lesson.title: Reading the Rock Archive: What Fossils Reveal About Life's History
lesson.summary: Fossils are the preserved physical remains or traces of once-living organisms, and their patterns in the rock record, what appears where and in what order, provide direct, physical evidence that life has changed over time.
lesson.body:
What a fossil actually is: preserved remains or traces (bones, shells, teeth, imprints, casts, even footprints and burrows called trace fossils) of organisms that lived in the past. Fossilization is rare. Normally, after death, decomposition and scavenging destroy soft tissue within days, and even hard parts like bone erode away over time. A fossil usually requires an unusual combination of events: rapid burial, in sediment, volcanic ash, tar, ice, or amber, that protects remains from decomposers and physical weathering, followed by chemical processes over long spans of time, such as minerals gradually replacing organic material, that turn the original structure into rock.

Because fossilization is rare and biased toward certain conditions (organisms with hard shells or bones in low-oxygen, sediment-rich environments like river deltas, lakebeds, and shallow seas), the fossil record is necessarily incomplete. Soft-bodied organisms, small populations, and organisms living in environments that do not favor burial are all underrepresented. Paleontologists take this incompleteness seriously. It is part of why the fossil record supports evolutionary history through pattern rather than by capturing every individual that ever lived. What matters is not that every ancestor is preserved, but that the fossils that were preserved, once arranged in time using the dating methods covered in the next chapter, tell a coherent and consistent story.

That story has two connected parts. First, order. When fossils are arranged from oldest layers to youngest, life's complexity and diversity change in a directional, non-random way. The oldest fossil-bearing rocks contain only simple, single-celled organisms, more complex multicellular life appears only in progressively younger layers, and lineages consistently appear, persist, and often disappear in ways that match relationships expected from common descent. You never find, for example, fossil rabbits in rock layers that predate the origin of mammals by hundreds of millions of years. That consistent absence of organisms appearing in the wrong order is itself strong evidence, because if fossils were distributed randomly with no evolutionary history connecting them, there would be no reason to expect such a consistent ordering.

Second, transitional fossils: specimens that show a mix of features from an older group and a more derived group, capturing evolutionary change in progress. A well documented example is the sequence of whale ancestors. Early fossils such as Pakicetus show a land mammal with features linking it to modern whales, and a series of later fossils, including Ambulocetus, Rodhocetus, and Basilosaurus, show, layer by layer through time, hind limbs shrinking, the nasal opening migrating backward toward the top of the skull, and the skeleton becoming progressively better adapted for a fully aquatic life. This series culminates in modern whales, which retain only tiny, reduced pelvic and leg bones, a structure covered later in this unit. Another well known example is Tiktaalik, a fossil fish with a flattened skull, a mobile neck, and limb-like fin bones, found in rock layers of just the age predicted for an intermediate between fish and the earliest four-limbed land vertebrates.

This chapter builds directly on the history of evolutionary thought. Naturalists like Georges Cuvier used fossil comparisons in the late 1700s and early 1800s to establish that extinction was a real, repeated phenomenon, a controversial idea at the time, and Charles Lyell's geological arguments for gradual, ongoing processes shaping the Earth over immense timescales gave Darwin the deep timescale he needed for gradual descent with modification to be plausible. The fossil record does not stand alone as evidence. Its patterns line up with the anatomical, embryological, biogeographic, and molecular evidence covered in the rest of this unit, and it is that convergence of independent lines of evidence, not any single fossil, that makes the case for evolution so strong.
